doc.title: Bill Allred interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 24, 2017

title: Booking gigs and the Daytona swing band price
summary: His first question to clients and the story of the Daytona customer who wanted a Lawrence Welk size band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Right. What’s the first question that you ask when someone calls with an inquiry about your band?

I usually ask them what do you want this music for. What do you want to accomplish. Is it a reunion, is it a wedding, which right away gives you a whole roomful of different people. So I said we’re going to have to play some swing, we’re going to have to play a little rock, which we never did. We usually would just play for the swing people. But yeah, you find out what they want, what kind of music they want. Then it naturally gravitates to how much you got to spend, or they ask you what you would charge them.
Yeah. That’s always the tough part for me.

Well I had a thing happen and I’ve got to tell you this. A guy called me from Daytona and he said, “Bill Allred, I understand you have a swing band.” And I said, “Yeah, we play all the swing stuff.” And he said, “Great,” he said, “my wife and I are celebrating

our 25th. She wants a swing band, so give me a price for your group.” And it was Daytona, it was a hotel, and I was trying to be fair, because we need to reach out a little bit in some of the different areas. So I gave him a fair price. So about a week later this same guy calls me, I forget his name, he said, “Bill Allred?” I said, “Yeah.” He said, “I’m the guy that called about the swing band.” I said, “Oh yeah.” He said, “I want to talk to you about your price.” So I’m thinking right away oh yeah, here we go you know, do you really need the bass player. And you get that.
Do you really need the bass player!

Yeah I’ve gotten that question. Well he said, “How many in that band?” I said, “There’s eight of us.” He said no, no, no. He said I want a band like Lawrence Welk. He says, “I want all the saxophones.” He said, “I want the same instrumentation. I want all the horns,” he said, “but I want a guy singer and a girl singer and I gotta have a guitar player.” And I’m doing some mental stuff. And he gets done with all that and I said, “Well Johnny” Johnny was his — “Johnny I said, the price I gave you was for eight guys, I said I’m going to have to re-do that and it’s going to be a lot higher.” He said, “Well figure it out and let me know because that’s what I know she would love.” You know. So I’m figuring it out and it’s getting up into many thousands. Sound man, because you get that many people then you’ve got to get a sound guy, we had to bring our own sound and stuff like that, and the book, and so he calls back a couple of days later and I gave him the price and he said, “Hmm,” he said, “that’s” and he reiterates, he said, “now it’s two singers, right.” I said, “I’ve got a really good gal and good guy from Disney, sings great, does all the crooner stuff.” Oh that’s great. And guitar player. I said it’s got a killer band. And I didn’t stick it to him, we gave everybody a fair wage and he said, “Let’s do it.” I couldn’t believe it. And we went over there and played great, they loved it, there were people coming in from other parties you know. That was a big band. And it was just amazing. He paid us, and he had dinner for everybody. And five years later they did the same thing again. And that’s the end, I’ve lost track. That was the total thing in reverse. Usually boy it’s a lot. Well Disney’s famous thing, Disney always wants to book a trio for everything.

That’s a good story. I’ve had occasion where I’ll give a price for a trio and then I’ll kick myself because the person will go, “Is that per man?” And that’s not what I meant, but well yes. It’s a little too late to do that.
